items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: I had the opportunity to play with him with John Coltrane in Chicago at the Plugged Nickel with Alice and Jimmy and Pharoah Sanders.

ctx.x: I had the fortunate circumstance of right next door to this office I’m sitting I had Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes here and that was just wonderful to listen to them talk about music and Rashied said something about, you know you’re talking about free jazz and many people think that it sounds angry. And he straightened me out on that, he just said it was the times we were in, it was a reflection of the times, and he did talk about the experiences he had in the military with segregation and so forth, and it was…

Yeah. Well you know I know Rashied and he’s very interesting. He’s a very musical drummer actually. And he found another way of playing, which was a multi — like a sound and a vibration that John Coltrane could play. I mean a lot of people, you know, not only he said it but Rashied used to play a lot of time. In fact I sat in on piano with him at his club Green Street. But he always carried a flute with him. So he’s very musical. But he discovered a way to play the drums in such a way that was very concentrated.…

And that was amazing. I learned a lot from Rashied just playing next to him. Because I was young and cocky and there I saw Rashied in terms of stamina and focus and concentration you know. I would play full out and then I’d get tired and stop and he’d be playing, he’d still be going. And I realized oh, he figured out a way to create the dynamics with a concentrated effort.

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: By then the band was Pharaoh Sanders, Alice on piano, Jimmy on bass and another drummer Rashied Ali. That was amazing, that week.

ctx.x: That was with the quartet? Elvin, McCoy, and Jimmy? Or Reggie?

Yeah. Each set they'd keep going higher and higher and higher. It's just awesome the level that it could get to. It got to beyond music, really. It got to some kind of spiritual uplifting feeling, you know? One night Elvin didn't make it back for the last set, so the place was packed. I've told this story quite a few times but it's a nice story. So, McKee was getting a little antsy and looking at his clock, people are waiting for the next set. So he said, "Coltrane! ctx.x: History Interview with NEA Jazz Master Jack DeJohnette. Now in his other studio, his recording studio! So Jack, when we left off yesterday we were talking about you joining the Miles Davis group. So, hopefully we can talk about some of that experience, because obviously that’s one the ones that really got you into the public, as everybody else who played with Miles launches their career into the public domain. Do you want to talk about the very first sessions that you were on? I think that’s where we left off. We…

Yeah. The time I spent was maybe three years, two or three years. It was kind of like a blur in a way. I think playing with Miles, with Dave Holland, Chick Corea and Wayne was a very exciting period. We always couldn’t wait to get on the bandstand to see what kind of mischief we could get into. In the studios… I get asked this question, “What was it like in the studio with Miles?” Especially during the period when he was doing In A Silent Way and Bitches Brew. Miles was in a very highly creative period where he…

would also be like Benny Maupin and Wayne. It was a flowing, organic session that Teo later edited and spliced together the best parts to sort of give it kind of a storyline, for lack of a better word. Miles had a penchant whenever he recorded, he recorded tempos, things that were slow because when he played these same tunes live they were always much faster. The studio versions were more relaxed.
